learn.intro: How revolutionary was industrialisation for children? And how successfully did Britain respond to the filth and disease it created? This topic uses real evidence about child labour, evaluates Oliver! as a later interpretation, and follows the public health reformers.

sections.title: 1. A child's revolution

blocks.p: Children worked long hours, often 12–14 hours a day, six days a week. In mills they pieced broken threads or crawled under machinery to clear blockages; in mines they worked as "trappers" opening ventilation doors or hauled coal tubs. Accidents from exhaustion and unguarded machines were common.
For many working-class families, children's wages were essential household income. That is context, not an excuse.

Government inquiries such as the Sadler Committee (1832) collected testimony from child workers. They are a key source, but were gathered to support reform, so historians read them with that purpose in mind.

Reform was gradual: the 1833 Factory Act limited children's hours and set minimum ages in textile mills (enforcement was patchy), and the 1842 Mines Act banned underground work for women and children under 10.

Oliver! (1968 film, based on Dickens's 1838 novel Oliver Twist) is a later interpretation, not evidence. It shows a workhouse and London pickpockets, not factory or mine work, so it blurs different experiences of poverty.

evidence: Sadler Committee 1832; Factory Act 1833; Mines Act 1842.
Oliver! (1968) is an interpretation, not evidence.

blocks.p: Industrial towns grew faster than any planning: no piped water, no sewage removal, a few outdoor toilets for dozens of families. Cholera, a waterborne disease, caused major epidemics in 1831–32, 1848–49 and 1854, killing tens of thousands.

ul: Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report used statistics to argue that poor sanitation caused disease and cost money. It helped lead to the 1848 Public Health Act, the first significant national public health law.
John Snow's 1854 investigation in Soho mapped cholera cases to the Broad Street water pump, evidence that cholera spread through water, not "bad air" (miasma). It took years to be accepted.
Joseph Bazalgette designed London's sewer network, built mainly in the 1860s after the "Great Stink" of 1858.

blocks.p: The response was gradual and contested. Many feared government interference and the cost, so change came slowly and unevenly. Did industrialisation solve the problems it created, or did government action?

misconceptions.wrong: Oliver! shows what factory child labour was like.
misconceptions.right: It shows a workhouse and pickpockets. It is a later interpretation, not evidence.

misconceptions.wrong: The 1833 Factory Act ended child labour.
misconceptions.right: It limited hours in textile mills; enforcement was patchy and other industries were not covered.
Miasma theory remained dominant for years.

misconceptions.wrong: Government acted quickly on public health.
misconceptions.right: Change was slow and contested because of cost and fear of interference.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "Industrialisation was revolutionary for children." How far do you agree? Use the four criteria.
questions.asks: Judge how revolutionary industrialisation was for children, using precise evidence and named criteria.
steps: Apply Scale and Depth to child labour evidence.
questions.plan: 3 minutes planning, 11 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.

model.t: Industrialisation was revolutionary for many children in depth, though not always positive.
Factory children often worked 12–14 hours a day under machine discipline, very different from work at home, as testimony to the Sadler Committee (1832) showed.
This meant the depth of change was great; reforms such as the 1833 Factory Act and 1842 Mines Act also show the change lasted long enough to force new laws.
Therefore it was revolutionary, but harmful for many children, showing that revolutionary does not mean positive.
